sections.history: Thiruvisanallur lies in the Kaveri delta a few kilometres east of Kumbakonam, in the Chola country north of the river. The Tevaram knows it as Tiruviyalur, and the hymn of the saint Sambandar, preserved in the First Thirumurai, makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. Local tradition says the Lord has borne a different name in each age: Purathaneswarar in the first, Vilvaranyeswarar in the second, Yoganandeeswarar in the third, and in the present age Sivayoganathar, the Lord of the yogis. The stone temple is Chola in character, and tradition associates it with the age of Rajaraja I, though its builders are not firmly documented. Cared for today by the Thanjavur Palace Devasthanam, it has been kept in worship for centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east, in the Dravidian manner of the Chola country, with towered gateways within a walled enclosure; one account counts five towers. The sanctum holds the Shiva linga of Sivayoganathar, and the goddess Soundara Nayaki, also called Santha Nayaki, is honoured in her own shrine. A curiosity that visitors remember is a sundial set into the outer wall, said to tell the hour with fair accuracy through the day, though it varies with the season. The temple tank is traditionally called Jatayu Teertham, after the great bird said to have worshipped here.
sections.legends: Tradition tells of eight Shiva yogis who sought liberation at this spot and merged into the linga, which is why the Lord is called Sivayoganathar, master of the yogis. Another tale concerns a king from the Malayalam country who had wronged many women and fell under their curse. A yogi sent him to this town; he bathed in the Kaveri, worshipped the Lord, and was freed, and so devotees come here seeking relief from such burdens. A third story recalls Nandi turning back Yama as he approached a devotee of Shiva, and the temple is held dear by those who pray for release from the fear of death. The tellings vary from one family of storytellers to another, but all circle the same truth: the Lord here gathers up what weighs on the heart.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is kept with worship through the night, and Pradosham and the Mondays of the week are held especially auspicious here. A celebrated observance of the village falls close by: on the new-moon day of Karthigai (November to December), thousands bathe at the well in the house of the saint Sridhara Ayyaval, now part of the Ayyaval Mutt, whose water is believed to carry the blessing of the Ganga. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Thiruvisanallur offers the quiet of a village temple a short way from the bustle of Kumbakonam. Enter from the east, come first to the sanctum of Sivayoganathar, and then to the gentle shrine of Soundara Nayaki. Look for the sundial on the outer wall and walk to the temple tank. Many devotees come to pray for peace of mind and freedom from fear, and a visit pairs naturally with the Ayyaval Mutt nearby, which is a separate site with its own well and its own customs.

visit.timings: Commonly reported as roughly 6 am to noon and 4 pm to 8 pm, though published timings vary slightly; confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thiruvisanallur is in Thanjavur district, about 10 km by road from Kumbakonam, which is the nearest railway station and the usual base for visitors. Tiruchirappalli has the nearest major airport. Local buses and autorickshaws run from Kumbakonam to the village.
